# What is biodiversity?

## What is biodiversity?

Variety and abundance of biological life

## What is biodiversity?

\spacedslide

Variety and abundance of biological life

 - There is no single definition or metric of biodiversity
 - Impossible to define succinctly or precisely
 - We typically do not include humans in estimates of biodiversity
 - The term is used loosely in the press

# Why do we monitor biodiversity? 

## Why do we monitor biodiversity?

\spacedslide

- To track how nature is changing
- To identify species or regions most at risk
- To identify causes of change
- To plan effective conservation action
- To track a community with one metric

## Why do we monitor biodiversity?

\spacedslide

Convention on Biological Diversity

Montreal, Canada, December 2022


\alert{TARGET 4}

Ensure urgent management actions to halt human induced extinction of known threatened species and for the recovery and conservation of species


\alert{TARGET 21}

Ensure that the best available data, information and knowledge, are accessible to decision makers, practitioners and the public 

## What is biodiversity? 

There are three scales at which biodiversity can be measured: 

 - \alert{$\alpha\ diversity$}: biodiversity at a local site and time 
 - \alert{$\beta\ diversity$}: biodiversity difference between sites or times  
 - \alert{$\gamma\ diversity$}: biodiversity across a region
 
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=1.65in,keepaspectratio]{figures/biodiversity/alpha_beta_gamma_div/Slide4}
\end{center}
 
\footnotesize
'local' = small enough that biodiversity can be accurately measured. 

## What is biodiversity? 

\spacedslide

There are typically three _types_ of biodiversity that can be measured: 

 - \alert{species richness}: number of species
      - of a defined taxonomic group (e.g. birds, butterflies, ants)
      - at a particular time (season, year)
      - BUT, we can't count ALL species (\alert{detectability!}), so how do we estimate this? 

 - \alert{evenness}: evenness or skewness of species abundances
      - is a community dominated by a single species or an even balance of species?
      - an exactly even balance is unrealistic in nature
      - how skewed / balanced is this community? 

 - \alert{diversity}: combination of richness and evenness


## What is biodiversity? 

\spacedslide

Clearly we need to know:

- Where animals are, and where they are not (distribution, occupancy)
- How many animals there are (abundance)

But how to measure these?

\alert{Monitoring surveys and methods for analysing the resulting data!}

## Estimating species presence

\spacedslide

\alert{Is a species present at a particular site during a defined period?}

- Reliable detections confirm presence, but not detecting a species does not prove absence
- Animals may be hidden, inactive or temporarily outside the surveyed area
- Repeated surveys help estimate \textbf{detectability}: the probability of detecting a species when it is present
- \textbf{Example:} Repeated camera surveys estimate which valleys ibex use, helping target protection and track changes in site use.

\footnotesize
Martin et al. (2007), \textit{Conservation Biology} 21:472--481; Nichols \& Williams (2006), \textit{Trends in Ecology \& Evolution} 21:668--673.

## Estimating species distributions

\spacedslide

\alert{Where does a species occur across a landscape?}

- Surveys tell us about sampled locations; distribution models link these records to habitat, elevation and other environmental variables
- Models predict where a species is likely to occur, including places we have not surveyed
- Maps help identify areas for protection, habitat restoration and further surveys
- \textbf{Example:} Otter sign surveys allow for predicting favourable habitat, helping to decide where to place future surveys.

## Estimating species abundance

\spacedslide

\alert{How many individuals are there, and where are they concentrated?}

- \textbf{Abundance}: number of individuals in a defined area and period; \textbf{density}: number per unit area
- A species can occur in many places but have most individuals concentrated in a few
- Johnston et al. found only \textbf{10--58\% overlap} between the top 50 sites selected using occurrence and relative abundance models for six waterbird species
- \textbf{Example:} Camera surveys and individual identification provide estimates of snow leopard population sizes and, if repeated over time, birth and death rates.

\footnotesize
Johnston et al. (2015), \textit{Ecological Applications} 25:1749--1756; Katzner et al. (2011), \textit{Animal Conservation} 14:328--332.

# What is monitoring?

## What is monitoring?

\spacedslide

\alert{Monitoring is planned, repeated measurement to answer a question about change.}

- One survey provides a \textbf{baseline}: an estimate of conditions at that time
- Comparable surveys repeated over time let us estimate changes in distribution, abundance or biodiversity
- Define the species, area, season, measurement and survey interval before starting
- Record survey effort and account for detectability so that changes in observations can be separated from changes in nature

\textbf{Example:} Estimate ibex density in selected valleys each autumn, before and after a change in grazing management.

\footnotesize
Nichols \& Williams (2006), \textit{Trends in Ecology \& Evolution} 21:668--673.

## Why monitor?

\spacedslide

- \alert{Plan conservation actions}
   - Identify priority species, places and seasons
   - Direct limited staff and funding to where actions can help most

- \alert{Evaluate conservation results}
   - Compare population responses with agreed objectives
   - More patrols or money spent do not, by themselves, demonstrate species recovery

- \alert{Learn and improve management}
   - Predict how populations might respond to alternative actions
   - Compare monitoring results with those predictions and use what we learn in the next decision

\footnotesize
Karanth et al., \textit{Role of Monitoring in Global Tiger Conservation}, Nichols \& Williams (2006).
  
## Good monitoring 

\spacedslide

\alert{Start with the decision or scientific question, then design the monitoring.}

- Agree on a conservation objective and the actions available
- State alternative explanations and predict responses to each action
- Choose measurements, sites and repeat visits that can distinguish those predictions; account for detectability and uncertainty
- Plan who will analyse the data, review results and use them in decisions

\textbf{Hypothetical example:} Will reduced livestock grazing increase ibex density? Monitor valleys with changed grazing and comparable valleys without the change, before and after management.

\textbf{Adaptive management:} act $\rightarrow$ monitor $\rightarrow$ compare predictions $\rightarrow$ update the next decision.

\footnotesize
Nichols \& Williams (2006), \textit{Trends in Ecology \& Evolution} 21:668--673.

## Bad monitoring

\spacedslide

- Collecting data without a clear question, analysis plan or route to conservation action
- Surveying only convenient sites, changing effort without recording it, or treating counts as the whole population
- Waiting for a statistically significant decline before considering action: detecting a trend can take years
- Detecting a decline but collecting no information to help evaluate possible remedies

\textbf{A warning from the US:} Estimated snail kite abundance fell by about \textbf{55\% from 1997 to 2005}. A single annual count failed to reveal the decline as detectability increased.

\footnotesize
Nichols \& Williams (2006); Martin et al. (2007), \textit{Conservation Biology} 21:472--481.

## Core principles

\spacedslide

:::: {.columns align="top"}

::: {.column width="49%"}

- \alert{Careful design of surveys and survey protocols}
   - Efficient allocation of survey effort
   - Field protocols
   - Data collection plan
   
- \alert{Using appropriate statistical methods}
   - Data requirements
   - Understanding and testing model assumptions 
   - Basic implementation with pointers to further reading

:::

::: {.column width="49%"}

- \alert{Reproducible workflow}
   - Data management plan and secure storage
   - Script-based statistical analysis (R)
   - Documenting all decisions made

- \alert{We use local species as case studies}
    - Species selected by project partners
    - Many of these already monitored in some form
    - All examples and data are hypothetical. Applications are necessarily simplified.

:::
